The sediments should provide a record of climatic and glacial flucuations, possibly data pertinent to understanding the causes of glaciation, and some knowledge of basins of deposition and the recent geologic history of the area. While there has been considerable progress made in the interpretation of the glacial history of the Antarctic continent, the record of these events found in continental deposits is usually incomplete and difficult to interpret. Numerous authors have suggested that the sediments on the continental shelf should provide answers to the many questions concerning the age and history of Antarctic glaciation.
Magnetic stratigraphy, paleontology, potassium-argon dating (if applicable), sedimentary petrology, sedimentology, and isotopic studies, not only of the RISP cores but from all other projects, should provide rather detailed information relating to the history of the Ross Sea Embayment and the adjoining portion of the continent. DSDP cores will provide clues as to possible past advances of the ice shelf, but only in the sediments beneath the ice will there be found clear evidence for less extensive phases of the ice shelf.
Sedimentary processes below ice shelves are completely unknown and extremely useful base information for interpreting past records such as are recorded in marine tillites throughout the geologic record may be obtained. The RISP sampling program will complement the DSDP drilling work in the Ross Sea and the DVDP drilling in the McMurdo and dry valley areas. logether these should combine to provide data of significance not only for local geologic studies but also for studies of worldwide fluctuations in glaciation and climate.
